title: Playing With People Better Than You
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece uses the decades-long rivalry between cyclists Wout Van Aert and Mathieu Van Der Poel to make a broader point about growth: people improve fastest when they regularly compete against, or work alongside, others who are more skilled than they are. The author argues that comfortable competition breeds complacency, while stretching against superior performers forces sharper preparation, practice, and attention to detail. The piece also cautions that the gap in skill shouldn't be so large that it undermines confidence. It closes by encouraging readers to deliberately seek out more skillful partners as part of their own development, while occasionally extending the same opportunity to those with less experience.
points: Cyclists Van Aert and Van Der Poel credit their rivalry, dating back to age nine, for pushing each other to elite performance.
Competing against more accomplished performers accelerates skill development in a way comfortable competition cannot.
The right challenge level matters: opponents should be better, but not so much better that confidence collapses.
Leaders and performers who study those ahead of them absorb superior habits of preparation and focus.
quotes: Those at any skill level make the most strides when they compete against others who are better than they are.
By holding themselves to a higher standard of performance, performers of any stripe begin to see things differently.
When not challenged by better performers, people come to rely on what they already know to succeed.
The key is to find performers who are better, but not so much so as to undermine confidence or to be overwhelmed by such advanced skills.
Dedicate a portion of your practice and play for those more skillful than you.
